Descriptive Statistics 1: Introduction to Statistics & Describing Data

Important⚠️ Note for video learners: {inspectdf} install instructions have changed

The package {inspectdf} was removed from CRAN and is no longer easily installed in R. Since recording, we’ve created a maintained fork of {inspectdf} on GitHub, so all the inspect_cat(), inspect_num(), inspect_types(), and show_plot() code in the video still works exactly as shown.

The only difference is how you install the package. Instead of pacman::p_load(inspectdf), use:

pacman::p_load_current_gh("the-graph-courses/inspectdf")

This is already included in the setup code at the top of these notes.

Introduction

In this lesson, we will:

  1. Introduce the key branches of statistics and their uses.

  2. Explore the fundamental concepts of descriptive analysis, focusing on:

    • Types of Variables: Numerical (continuous, discrete) and Categorical (ordinal, nominal)

    • Graphical Summaries for each type.

    • Numerical Summaries for categorical variables.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Understand the key branches of statistics: descriptive and inferential.
  2. Explain the aims and methods of descriptive statistics.
  3. Identify numerical and categorical variables and their subtypes.
  4. Create appropriate graphical summaries for each variable type in R, using {ggplot2}, {visdat}, and {inspectdf}.
  5. Create numerical summaries for categorical variables.
  6. Visually assess skew and symmetry in data distributions.

What is Statistics?

“The science of collecting, summarising, presenting and interpreting data, and of using them to estimate the magnitude of associations and test hypotheses.” (Kirkwood & Sterne, 2003).

Two Key Branches of Statistics

Descriptive statistics involves the organization, summarization, and display of data (e.g., tables, charts, numerical summary statistics).

Inferential statistics involves using sample data to draw conclusions about a population.

Population and Samples

Before diving deeper, let’s briefly cover the concepts of populations and samples.

Population

A population refers to the entire set of individuals or items that we are interested in studying.

  • Example: Calculating the true average height of all adult women in a country would require measuring every adult woman in the country.

Sample

A sample is a subset of the population, selected for practical reasons, from which we infer characteristics of the entire population.

  • Example: Studying the height of 1,000 randomly selected adult women from a part of the country.
TipPopulation vs. Sample
Population Sample
Includes all members of a specified group Subset of the population
Often impractical to study entirely Practical and feasible to study
Example: All residents in France Example: 1,000 randomly chosen residents in Paris

We can almost never measure every single unit in a population, so we use sample data to estimate the true population parameters.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse,

pacman::p_load_current_gh("the-graph-courses/inspectdf")

The Yaounde COVID-19 dataset

In this lesson, we analyse results from a COVID-19 serological survey conducted in Yaounde, Cameroon in late 2020. The survey estimated how many people had been infected with COVID-19 in the region, by testing for IgG and IgM antibodies. The full dataset can be obtained from Zenodo, and the paper can be viewed here.

Spend some time browsing through this dataset. Each line corresponds to one patient surveyed. There are some demographic, socio-economic and COVID-related variables. The results of the IgG and IgM antibody tests are in the columns igg_result and igm_result.

# Import data to RStudio
yaounde <- read_csv(here("data/yaounde_data.csv"))

Note that glimpse() reports numeric variables as <dbl> (double, for values that can include decimals) or <int> (integer, for whole numbers only). Character variables (with text values) are shown as <chr>. R does not automatically know whether a categorical variable is ordinal or not - all text variables come in as <chr> by default, and we’ll convert specific ones to ordered factors later in the lesson.

We can also visualize the R data type of each variable in our dataset using vis_dat() from the {visdat} package. Each column represents a column in our data frame, and the color tells us the R data class.

# VISUALIZE DATA TYPE OF EACH VARIABLE
vis_dat(yaounde)

We can further investigate just the categorical and the numeric variables separately using functions from {inspectdf}.

# INSPECT CATEGORICAL VARIABLES
yao_cat_summary <- inspect_cat(yaounde)
show_plot(yao_cat_summary)
Tip

In RStudio, you can click on yao_cat_summary in the Environment tab and then click on the levels column to see the exact count for every category of each variable (e.g., 635 adults, 291 children, 45 seniors in age_category_3).

# INSPECT NUMERIC VARIABLES
yao_num_summary <- inspect_num(yaounde)
show_plot(yao_num_summary)

Notice that some “is_drug” variables show up as numeric (with 0s and 1s) even though they are really binary categorical variables. We can convert them to logical type using as.logical().

# Convert "is_drug" variables to logical
yao2 <- yaounde %>% 
  mutate(across(starts_with("is_drug"), as.logical))

Now if we re-run inspect_num() on yao2, we see histograms of only the true numeric variables:

show_plot(inspect_num(yao2))

We can also look at vis_dat() again to see the data types after conversion:

vis_dat(yao2)

Now let’s use mutate() to convert several variables to their correct R data classes all at once:

yaounde <- yaounde %>%  
  mutate(across(starts_with("is_drug"), as.logical),
         across(starts_with("n_"), as.integer),
         age_category_3 = factor(age_category_3,
                                 levels = c("Child", "Adult", "Senior")), 
         is_smoker = factor(is_smoker,
                            levels = c("Non-smoker", "Ex-smoker", "Smoker")),
         highest_education = factor(highest_education,
                                    levels = c("No formal instruction", 
                                               "Primary",
                                               "Secondary",
                                               "University",
                                               "Doctorate",
                                               "No response"))
         )

Let’s verify the changes using vis_dat():

vis_dat(yaounde)

We can also use inspect_types() from {inspectdf} to get a summary of the different variable types in our data frame:

show_plot(inspect_types(yaounde))
TipWhat is a variable?

A variable is something we can observe or study, a feature of individual units (e.g., humans) in our data.

Variable Types

When conducting descriptive analysis, the method you choose will depend on the type of data you’re analyzing. At the most basic level, variables can be described as numerical or categorical.

Numeric variables can then be further divided into continuous and discrete - the distinction being whether the variable can take on a continuum of values (e.g., height or weight), or only set of certain values (e.g., age or year).

Categorical variables can be subdivided into ordinal or nominal variables - depending on whether or not the categories can logically be ordered in a meaningful way.

Some examples of categorical variables seen in our yaounde data frame are: sex, highest_education, and age_category. In fact, most of the variables in this dataset are categorical.

head(yaounde)

Can you identify which variables are numeric? Of those, which are continuous and which are discrete? The glimpse() function can help us get a better look at this.

TipReview of the Main Data Types in R

Each variable type corresponds to different R data classes/types:

Variable Type R Data Type
Continuous numeric, specifically double
Discrete numeric, specifically integer
Nominal character
Ordinal factor (ordered)
Binary

  • numeric, specifically integer with 2 values (e.g., 0 and 1)

  • logical a.k.a. Boolean (TRUE or FALSE)

  • character with 2 values (e.g., “success” and “failure”)

  • factor with 2 values, (e.g., “low” and “high”)

Reordering the age_category variable

The age_category variable (the 5-level version) is currently a character variable, so ggplot sorts it alphabetically on bar charts. Use mutate() and factor() to reorder it by age (youngest to oldest), then re-plot the bar chart to confirm the ordering is correct.

Methods of Describing Distributions

Variables in a dataset are described by distributions rather than single values.

Remember, we are ultimately aiming to make inferences about populations rather than individuals, so we are not just interested in describing one particular person, but the population as a whole.

How do we describe distributions? One option is to display all the data, but that is not necessarily useful or practical.

Descriptive analysis of numerical variables can be measured by two different methods: graphical or numerical. The best way to describe a distribution depends on the type of variable being summarized and its distribution.

  1. Graphical methods (e.g., tables, charts)
    • Categorical variables
      • Nominal (no inherent order, e.g., gender, country)
        • Bar chart or pie chart
      • Ordinal (clear order, e.g., Likert scale: poor, fair, good)
        • Bar chart with ordered categories
    • Numerical variables
      • Continuous (those that can take any value, e.g., heights and weights)
        • Histogram
        • Density curve
        • Box plot or violin plot
      • Discrete (integer counts, e.g., number of cases, age)
        • Bar chart
        • Histogram with integer bins
  2. Numerical methods (i.e., summarizing the data in a small number of key values – summary statistics)
    • Categorical variables
      • Ordinal or Nominal
        • Frequencies or counts
        • Proportions or percentages
    • Numerical variables
      • Discrete
        • Frequency/counts and proportions
        • Discrete distributions
        • Cumulative frequency (?)
      • Continuous
        • Measures of Central Tendency (e.g., mean, median, variance)
        • Measures of Dispersion (e.g., range, variance, standard deviation)
TipHow do we describe distributions?

There are both numerical and graphical methods we can use to perform descriptive analysis for all types and subtypes of variables.

Variable Types (Fill‑in‑the‑Blanks)

Complete each sentence with the most appropriate term:

  1. Quantitative variables are called ________, whereas qualitative variables are called ________.

  2. Binary variables have exactly ____ categories.

  3. ________ categorical variables contain groups that cannot be meaningfully ordered.

  4. Discrete numeric variables consist of whole numbers, also referred to as ________.

  5. Long ordinal variables can often be treated as ___________, if they have sufficient categories and are relatively evenly distributed.

Categorical Variables

We’ll start by describing categorical variables, both numerically and graphically. As a reminder, categorical variables are variables whose values fit into distinct categories.

Numerical Descriptions of Categorical Variables

We’ll begin our discussion of descriptive statistics in the categorical half of our flow chart. Specifically, we’ll start by numerically describing categorical variables.

The two most common numerical descriptions of categorical variables are probably the frequency count (you will often hear this referred to as simply the frequency, the count, or the n) and the proportion or percentage (the percentage is just the proportion multiplied by 100).

Using the tabyl() function from the {janitor} package, we can make frequency tables displaying the frequencies and percentages of categorical variable(s).

# Make a frequency table of the `is_smoker` variable.
yaounde %>% tabyl(is_smoker)
  is_smoker   n     percent valid_percent
 Non-smoker 859 0.884654995    0.88648091
  Ex-smoker  71 0.073120494    0.07327141
     Smoker  39 0.040164779    0.04024768
       <NA>   2 0.002059732            NA

The count (n column) is simply the number of observations, in this case deaths, which fall into each possible category.

The proportion (percentage column) is just the count divided by the total number of observations. In this example, almost 9 out of 10 deaths (.87 or 87%) died in a hospital or clinic.

The valid_percent column removes NAs from the denominator. In is_smoker there are only a few NAs so this won’t differ much from percent, but let’s try it with is_pregnant, which has many NAs:

yaounde %>% tabyl(is_pregnant)
 is_pregnant   n    percent valid_percent
          No 464 0.47785788    0.84517304
 No response  61 0.06282183    0.11111111
         Yes  24 0.02471679    0.04371585
        <NA> 422 0.43460350            NA

Now you can see a big difference between percent and valid_percent. There are 422 NAs in this variable, so although only about 47% of total responses were “No”, 85% of valid respondents were not pregnant.

We can also use the tabyl() function to create 2-way frequency tables (i.e., contingency tables or cross-tabulations).

# Create a summary data frame of two categorical variables
yaounde %>%
  tabyl(is_smoker, sex)
  is_smoker Female Male
 Non-smoker    528  331
  Ex-smoker     16   55
     Smoker      4   35
       <NA>      1    1
yaounde %>%
  tabyl(is_smoker, sex) %>%
  adorn_percentages("row")
  is_smoker    Female      Male
 Non-smoker 0.6146682 0.3853318
  Ex-smoker 0.2253521 0.7746479
     Smoker 0.1025641 0.8974359
       <NA> 0.5000000 0.5000000

Let’s try this with two other variables. Remember the pregnancy variable had a lot of NAs - is that connected to sex?

yaounde %>%
  tabyl(is_pregnant, sex) %>%
  adorn_percentages("row")
 is_pregnant Female Male
          No      1    0
 No response      1    0
         Yes      1    0
        <NA>      0    1

Looking at the row proportions, we can see that 100% of the NAs are in the male column. To see the raw counts behind this, we can drop adorn_percentages():

yaounde %>%
  tabyl(is_pregnant, sex)
 is_pregnant Female Male
          No    464    0
 No response     61    0
         Yes     24    0
        <NA>      0  422

All 422 NAs were males, which is exactly why the percent and valid_percent columns differed in the one-way pregnancy table we made earlier.

Use the tabyl() function from the {janitor} package to answer the following:

  1. Create a frequency table of has_contact_covid.

  2. Create a two-way frequency table between has_contact_covid and igg_result.

Graphical Descriptions of Categorical Variables

A bar chart is the simplest way to graphically describe the distribution of a categorical variable.

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = is_smoker))

A stacked bar chart can help us visualize the distribution of two categorical variables.

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = is_smoker, fill = sex))

A percent-stacked bar chart visualizes them as proportions rather than counts.

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = is_smoker, fill = sex),
    position = "fill"
  )

We can add count labels inside the bars and total counts above each bar using geom_text():

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = is_smoker, fill = sex),
    position = "fill"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = is_smoker, label = after_stat(count), group = sex),
    stat = "count",
    position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white"
  )  +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = is_smoker, label = paste("n =", after_stat(count))),
    stat = "count",
    position = position_fill(vjust = 1.05)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Smoking Status", y = "Proportion", fill  = "Sex",
    title = "Smoking Status by Sex"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#1f77b4", "Female" = "#ff7f0f"))

We can also use position = "dodge" to create side-by-side bar charts instead of stacked:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = is_smoker, fill = sex),
    position = "dodge"
  )

We can also swap the stratification hierarchy. So instead of a bar chart of is_smoker filled by sex, we can make a bar chart of sex filled by is_smoker:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = sex, fill = is_smoker),
    position = "fill"
  )

It is generally a good idea to look at the data both ways. If the focus of your research is to compare males and females, you’d probably want this graph. If the focus is to compare smokers, ex-smokers, and non-smokers, the previous graph is more appropriate.

Bar chart of an ordinal variable with ordered categories

By default, ggplot orders categorical variables alphabetically on the x-axis. Let’s see what happens with highest_education:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = highest_education))

Because we already converted highest_education to a factor with ordered levels earlier, the categories now appear in a meaningful order (from “No formal instruction” up to “Doctorate”) rather than alphabetically. If we had used yao2 instead - where highest_education is still a character variable - the bars would be sorted alphabetically. This is why setting up factors with the correct level order matters for plotting.

For reference, here is the factor conversion (already done earlier in the lesson):

yaounde <- yaounde %>%
  mutate(
    highest_education =
      factor(highest_education,
        levels = c(
          "No formal instruction",
          "Primary",
          "Secondary",
          "University",
          "Doctorate",
          "No response"
        )
      )
  )

Stratification - compare distributions between categories

We can stratify the bar chart by sex to compare the distributions of education levels between males and females:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = highest_education, fill = sex))

We see that secondary education is the most common education level overall. But because the total numbers of males and females in the data aren’t equal, raw counts can be misleading. Let’s switch to proportions:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = highest_education, fill = sex),
    position = "fill"
  )

Now we can see a clear pattern: at the lowest education level (no formal instruction), the bar is mostly female. As we move up through primary, secondary, university, and doctorate, the proportion of males increases and eventually overtakes the proportion of females.

Swap the stratification hierarchy

We can also flip which variable is on the x-axis and which is the fill:

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = sex, fill = highest_education),
    position = "fill"
  )

This view emphasizes the distribution of education levels within each sex, rather than the distribution of sexes within each education level. As before, the choice depends on which comparison is the focus of your analysis.

Bar Charts

Use ggplot() to create the following charts:

  1. Plot a bar chart showing the distribution of age_category_3, colored by igg_result.

  2. Create a percent-stacked bar chart showing the same variables.

  3. Add text labels to show the count of individuals in each age group, using geom_text(). Customize the look of the plot as desired (titles, labels, and colors).

Numerical Variables

Graphical Summaries of Numerical Variables

Visualizations are essential in public health to communicate findings clearly. Two common plots for numerical data are histograms and boxplots.

Histograms

A histogram shows how often values fall into specified bins or intervals. This is useful for checking skewness and identifying outliers.

A histogram visualizes the distribution of a numerical value as follows:

  1. We first cut up the x-axis into a series of bins, where each bin represents a range of values.
  2. For each bin, we count the number of observations that fall in the range corresponding to that bin.
  3. Then for each bin, we draw a bar whose length marks the corresponding count.
Tip

The function for creating histogram in {ggplot2} is geom_histogram(). We can use fill and color to enhance the appearance of the bars.

Now let’s use {ggplot2} to plot the distribution of heights, which is recorded in the height_cm column.

# Histogram showing the distribution of height_cm
ggplot(
  data = yaounde,
  mapping = aes(x = height_cm)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    color = "white",
    fill = "steelblue", binwidth = 5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 12),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
  • The histogram shows how the probabilities of measurements are distributed.
  • The tallest part of the histogram shows the region where measurements are more likely.
  • Most of the measurements come from people between 150 and 180 cm tall.
  • This is a slightly left-skewed distribution, probably because of a few children who are on the shorter side.

What if we filter out the children and plot the histogram again?

# Create new df of only adults
yao_adults <- yaounde %>% filter(age_category_3 != "Child")

# Define base ggplot layers
yao_adults_height <- ggplot(
  data = yao_adults,
  mapping = aes(x = height_cm)
) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 12),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    color = "white",
    fill = "steelblue",
    binwidth = 5
  )
  • We have a much more normal distribution, which is what you would expect for a variable like height or weight.
  • Note the outliers: 2 adults under 140 cm.

We can add count labels to each bin using geom_text() with stat = "bin" to see exact counts:

yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    color = "white",
    fill = "steelblue",
    binwidth = 5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = after_stat(count)),
    stat = "bin",
    binwidth = 5,
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3
  )

If we narrow the x-axis limits, we can see that the distribution is nearly symmetrical without the outliers:

yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    color = "white",
    fill = "steelblue",
    binwidth = 5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 12),
    expand = c(0, 0),
    limits = c(130, 190)
  )

Note: ggplot will warn that it removed rows outside the scale range. Generally, it is not a good idea to hide parts of your data, but this demonstrates that the outliers are the source of skew.

We can vary the number of bins to get more or less detail from the histogram.

# Try different numbers of bins

yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 3,
    color = "white",
    fill = "steelblue"
  )
yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    color = "white",
    fill = "cornflowerblue"
  )
yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    color = "white",
    fill = "dodgerblue"
  )
  • By using smaller bins, we get a more accurate and precise estimate of how heights are distributed.

Density Curves

  • We can also represent continuous distributions with a smoothed curve, which is a useful alternative to the histogram.
  • We can use a curve to approximate the histogram by plotting it on top of the bars.
yao_adults_height +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    color = "white",
    fill = "dodgerblue",
    mapping = aes(y = after_stat(density))
  ) +
  geom_density(
    color = "indianred2",
    alpha = 0.25,
    linewidth = 1,
    bw = 3
  )

The curve tells us the same thing that the histogram tells us:

  • People shorter than 155 cm were relatively rare - i.e., there is a low probability that we will measure an adult shorter than 155 cm.
  • People taller than 175 cm were also relatively rare - i.e., there is a low probability that we will measure an adult taller than 175 cm.

The curve has a few advantages over the histogram.

  • For example, we don’t have any values in the second-last bin, but we can use the curve to calculate the probability.
  • Furthermore, the curve is not limited by the width of the bins - we can use calculus to determine the probability of measuring someone between 172.5 and 183.7 cm, without having to round to the nearest bin size.
  • Lastly, if we have very few measurements, we can still approximate a curve using the mean and standard deviation of the few data points that we have.
ggplot(
  data = sample_n(yao_adults, 100),
  mapping = aes(x = height_cm)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    color = "white",
    fill = "dodgerblue",
    mapping = aes(y = after_stat(density))
  ) +
  geom_density(
    color = "indianred2",
    alpha = 0.25,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 24),
    expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(70 , 200)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(height_cm)),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1
  )

Try rerunning the code; each time will use a different random sample of 100 individuals from the dataset.

TipStratifying kernel density plots

The geom_density() function draws kernel density estimates, which is a smoothed version of a histogram. This is a useful alternative to the histogram for continuous data.

By plotting separate overlapping curves for each sex, we can graphically describe how the distribution of heights varies between sexes.

ggplot(yao_adults, aes(height_cm,
  colour = sex,
  fill = sex
)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.1)

Boxplots

Let’s start with a simple boxplot by mapping one numeric variable from yaounde, the height of patients (height_cm).

# Simple boxplot of height_cm
ggplot(
  data = yaounde,
  mapping = aes(x = height_cm)
) +
  geom_boxplot()

A boxplot consists of two parts:

  1. Box — Extends from the first to the third quartile (Q1 to Q3) with a line in the middle that represents the median. The range of values between Q1 and Q3 is also known as an Interquartile range (IQR).
  2. Whiskers — Lines extending from both ends of the box indicate variability outside Q1 and Q3. The minimum/maximum whisker values are calculated as \(Q1 - 1.5 \times IQR\) to \(Q3 + 1.5 \times IQR\) . Everything outside is represented as an outlier using dots or other markers.
Tip

The function for creating boxplots in {ggplot2} is geom_boxplot(). We can use fill argument inside the aes() function to color the boxes by a categorical variable.

To create a side-by-side boxplot (which is what we usually want), we need to add a categorical variable.

Let’s split height_cm by the sex variable.

ggplot(
  yaounde,
  aes(
    x = sex,
    y = height_cm,
    fill = sex
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot()

We can also use coord_flip() to swap the axes for a horizontal orientation:

ggplot(
  yaounde,
  aes(
    x = sex,
    y = height_cm,
    fill = sex
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()

We can clearly see that there are notable differences in median height (central line of each box) between sexes. However, there is a lot of overlap between the range of values.

Boxplots have the limitation that they summarize the data into just five numbers: the 1st quartile, the median (the 2nd quartile), the 3rd quartile, and the upper and lower whiskers. By doing this, we might miss important characteristics of the data.

One way to add more detail is to plot the individual observations as a layer of points on top of the boxplot with the geom_jitter() function.

ggplot(
  yaounde,
  aes(
    x = sex,
    y = height_cm,
    fill = sex
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color = sex)) +
  geom_jitter(
    size = 2,
    width = 0.25,
    alpha = 0.3
  )

Here, additional patterns become visible, such as variations and potential outliers within each sex group.

You can try out different variations of stratifying boxplots. Here we use facet_wrap() to create side-by-side plots for each sex, with age category on the x-axis:

# Comparing distributions across sub categories
ggplot(yaounde, aes(x = age_category_3, y = height_cm,
    fill = age_category_3,
    shape = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~sex)

In both panels, children show a much wider range of heights than adults and seniors - which makes sense, since children are still growing. Once people reach adulthood, height stabilizes, so the boxes for adults and seniors are much more compact. We can also see that adult males are taller than adult females on average. Interestingly, for children, the median height is similar between sexes (and actually slightly lower for male children in this sample).

Violin Plots

An alternative to boxplots are violin plots. Similarly to how a density curve is an alternative to a histogram, a violin plot is like a density curve mirrored on both sides.

# Density curve mirrored on the sides
ggplot(yaounde, aes(x = age_category_3, y = height_cm,
    fill = age_category_3,
    shape = sex)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_wrap(~sex)

The width of each “violin” at a given height value reflects how many observations have that height - so the widest parts of the violin correspond to the most common heights. For adult females, the densest region falls between 150 and 175 cm (peak around 160 cm), and for adult males the peak sits a bit higher, around 175 cm. This matches what we saw earlier in the histograms and density curves.

# Add points to see individual observations
ggplot(yaounde, aes(x = age_category_3, y = height_cm,
    fill = age_category_3,
    shape = sex)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5, aes(color = age_category_3))

Overlaying the individual points makes it clear when small bumps or bulges in a violin are driven by just a handful of observations - a useful sanity check, since the smoothed curve can otherwise make small clusters of points look more substantial than they really are.

TipAdding mean markers to a boxplot

You may want to visualize the mean (average) value of the distributions on a boxplot.

We can do this by adding a statistics layer using the stat_summary() function.

# Add a marker to show the mean
ggplot(
  yaounde,
  aes(
    x = sex, height_cm,
    y = height_cm,
    fill = sex,
    color = sex
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = "mean",
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    shape = 23,
    fill = "white"
  )

Graphical methods for numeric variables

We measured the age of 10,000 women in the UK. How would you suggest we look at the distribution of age across the sample population?

  1. Produce a bar chart, with age across the x-axis and frequency on the y-axis
  2. Produce a frequency table with all the ages in ascending order
  3. Produce a histogram using age bins
  4. Produce a bar chart, with age across the x-axis and gender across the y-axis

Key Takeaways

  • Descriptive statistics is the first step before any inferential analysis. It involves investigating variable types and their distributions.
  • Variables are classified as numerical (continuous or discrete) or categorical (ordinal or nominal), and each type has appropriate graphical and numerical summaries.
  • R data classes (numeric, character, factor, logical, Date) correspond to variable types, and it is important to convert variables to the correct class before analysis.
  • Graphical summaries (histograms, density curves, boxplots, violin plots, bar charts) reveal patterns not always evident from numerical summaries alone.
  • Numerical summaries (frequency tables, proportions) provide precise values for categorical distributions.

In the next lesson, we will continue our deep dive into numerical variables by covering measures of central tendency (mean, median, and mode) and how to calculate and interpret them in R.

Answer Key

Variable Types (Multiple-Choice)

For each of the four variables below, state whether it is numerical or categorical. If the variable is categorical, specify if it’s ordinal or nominal. If numerical, classify as discrete or continuous.

  1. Stress level, responses are “high”, “medium”, “low”. Categorical – Ordinal
  2. Age in years. Numerical – Discrete
  3. Height in centimeters. Numerical – Continuous
  4. Country name. Categorical – Nominal

Variable Types (Fill‑in‑the‑Blanks)

Complete each sentence with the most appropriate term:

  1. Quantitative variables are called numeric, whereas qualitative variables are called categorical.

  2. Binary variables have exactly two categories.

  3. Nominal categorical variables contain groups that cannot be meaningfully ordered.

  4. Discrete numeric variables consist of whole numbers, also referred to as integers.

  5. Long ordinal variables can often be treated as continuous/numeric, if they have sufficient categories and are relatively evenly distributed.

Identifying Variable Types and R Data Classes

  1. age – Numerical (Discrete), R class: Numeric
  2. highest_education – Categorical (Ordinal), R class: Character or Factor
  3. is_smoker – Categorical (Nominal), R class: Character
  4. date_surveyed – Date, R class: Date
  5. weight_kg – Numerical (Continuous), R class: Numeric
  6. igg_result – Categorical (Nominal), R class: Character

R data classes correspond to different variable types:

Variable Type R Data Class Example Variables in Yaounde Dataset
Continuous Numeric height_cm, weight_kg
Discrete Integer, Numeric age, n_days_miss_work
Ordinal Factor (ordered) highest_education
Nominal Factor, Character sex, neighborhood
Logical Logical is_pregnant, is_medicated
Date Date date_surveyed

Reordering the age_category variable

yaounde <- yaounde %>%
  mutate(
    age_category = factor(age_category,
      levels = c("5 - 14", "15 - 29", "30 - 44", "45 - 64", "65+")
    )
  )

ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = age_category))

Frequency Tables

Use the tabyl() function from the {janitor} package to answer the following:

  1. Create a frequency table of has_contact_covid.
yaounde %>% tabyl(has_contact_covid)
          has_contact_covid   n    percent
           No COVID contact 705 0.72605561
       Recent COVID contact  35 0.03604531
 Unsure about COVID contact 231 0.23789907
  1. Create a two-way frequency table between has_contact_covid and igg_result.
yaounde %>% tabyl(
  has_contact_covid,
  igg_result
)
          has_contact_covid Negative Positive
           No COVID contact      502      203
       Recent COVID contact       19       16
 Unsure about COVID contact      148       83
  1. Use adorn_percentages("row") to display row-wise proportions in the table created above.
yaounde %>%
  tabyl(
    has_contact_covid,
    igg_result
  ) %>%
  adorn_percentages("row")
          has_contact_covid  Negative  Positive
           No COVID contact 0.7120567 0.2879433
       Recent COVID contact 0.5428571 0.4571429
 Unsure about COVID contact 0.6406926 0.3593074

Bar Charts

Use ggplot() to create the following charts:

  1. Plot a bar chart showing the distribution of age_category_3, colored by igg_result.
ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = age_category_3, fill = igg_result))
  1. Create a percent-stacked bar chart showing the same variables.
ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = age_category_3, fill = igg_result),
    position = "fill"
  )
  1. Add text labels to show the count of individuals in each age group, using geom_text(). Customize the look of the plot as desired (titles, labels, and colors).
ggplot(yaounde) +
  geom_bar(
    aes(
      x = age_category_3,
      fill = igg_result
    ),
    position = "fill"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = age_category_3, label = after_stat(count), group = igg_result),
    stat = "count",
    position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white"
  )  +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = age_category_3, label = paste("n =", after_stat(count))),
    stat = "count",
    position = position_fill(vjust = 1.05)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Age Group", y = "Proportion", fill  = "COVID Status",
    title = "COVID Status across Age Groups",
    subtitle = "Survey of urban residents in Yaounde, Cameroon (Oct-Nov 2020)",
    caption = "Data source: Nwosu et. al. (2021) Nature Communications"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Negative" = "indianred", "Positive" = "dodgerblue")) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0.05))

Histograms

  • Plot a histogram showing the distribution of n_bedridden_days in yaounde.
ggplot(
  data = yaounde,
  mapping = aes(x = n_bedridden_days)
) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue")

Make notes on these key questions:

  1. What are the smallest and largest values?
  2. What are frequent and infrequent values?
  • Smallest value is 0.
  • Largest may be 30, but it is an outlier.
  • Most frequent value is 0.
  • Distribution is heavily left-skewed, with most patients having no or very few bedridden days.

Density Plot: weight by sex

  • Plot a kernel density plot showing the distribution of weight for each sex in yaounde.
ggplot(yaounde, aes(weight_kg,
  colour = sex,
  fill = sex
)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.1)

Using yao_adults:

ggplot(yao_adults, aes(weight_kg,
  colour = sex,
  fill = sex
)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.1)
  • Shows typical weight slightly differs by sex.
  • Distributions largely overlap.
  • In yaounde (with children): distribution is bimodal - with two peaks. Perhaps one for children and one for adults.
  • In yao_adults (without children): distribution becomes unimodal with a single clear peak.
  • Males have a slightly higher central tendency.

Boxplots

  • Create a boxplot showing the distribution of weights for each sex. Improve the plot by adding a layer of jittered points and a marker for the mean.
ggplot(
  yaounde,
  aes(
    x = sex,
    y = weight_kg,
    fill = sex,
    color = sex
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = "mean",
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    shape = 23,
    fill = "white"
  )

Appendix: R functions used in this lesson

  • Data Import & Setup
    • read_csv()
      Reads CSV files into a data frame (from the readr package).
    • here()
      Constructs file paths relative to the project’s root (from the here package).
  • Data Exploration & Inspection
    • spec()
      Retrieves the full column specification of a data frame (from readr).
    • str()
      Displays the structure of a data frame in a compact format (base R).
    • glimpse()
      Displays the structure of a data frame in a tidyverse-friendly format (from dplyr/tibble).
    • head()
      Shows the first few rows of a data frame.
    • vis_dat()
      Visualizes the data types of each variable in a data frame (from the visdat package).
    • inspect_cat()
      Summarizes categorical variables in a data frame (from the inspectdf package).
    • inspect_num()
      Summarizes numeric variables in a data frame (from the inspectdf package).
    • inspect_types()
      Summarizes the count of each data type in a data frame (from the inspectdf package).
    • show_plot()
      Displays a visual summary of inspected data (from the inspectdf package).
  • Data Manipulation & Summary
    • %>%
      The pipe operator for chaining operations (from magrittr or dplyr).
    • mutate()
      Creates or transforms variables in a data frame (from dplyr).
    • across()
      Applies a function across multiple columns (from dplyr).
    • filter()
      Subsets rows based on conditions (from dplyr).
    • factor()
      Converts a variable to a factor with specified levels (base R).
    • as.logical()
      Converts a variable to logical type (base R).
    • as.integer()
      Converts a variable to integer type (base R).
    • tabyl()
      Creates frequency tables, showing counts (and can compute percentages) for categorical variables (from the janitor package).
    • adorn_percentages()
      Adds percentage calculations to frequency tables (from the janitor package).
  • Data Visualization (using ggplot2)
    • ggplot()
      Initializes a ggplot object.
    • aes()
      Sets up aesthetic mappings in ggplot2 plots.
    • geom_bar()
      Creates bar charts.
    • geom_histogram()
      Creates histograms.
    • geom_density()
      Creates kernel density plots.
    • geom_boxplot()
      Creates boxplots.
    • geom_violin()
      Creates violin plots.
    • geom_jitter()
      Adds jittered points to a plot to show individual observations.
    • geom_text()
      Adds text labels to a plot.
    • stat_summary()
      Adds summary statistics (e.g., mean markers) as a layer in a plot.
    • facet_wrap()
      Creates small multiples, splitting a plot by a categorical variable.
    • coord_flip()
      Swaps the x and y axes of a plot.
    • scale_fill_manual()
      Manually sets fill colors for aesthetic mappings.
